paragraphs: Causal inference asks questions that require more than identifying patterns in observed data. This paper investigates how far such inference can go without substantive assumptions. It introduces topologies on spaces of structural causal models, giving a mathematical framework for studying which causal conclusions can be learned and what assumptions make them possible.

The central result is a topological causal hierarchy theorem: substantive causal inference without assumptions is possible only within a meager set of models. Here, meager describes smallness in a topological sense; it is not a numerical probability assigned to those models. The authors also connect their framework to an established relationship between open sets in the weak topology and statistically verifiable hypotheses.

Through that connection, the paper shows that inductive assumptions sufficient for valid causal inference are statistically unverifiable in principle. The result clarifies why assumptions are unavoidable, rather than making causal inference pointless. The framework also accommodates infinitely many variables, and the authors suggest it could help researchers compare alternative causal assumptions.
neurips-2021-a-topological-perspective-o.tldr: A topological analysis shows why substantive causal inference generally requires assumptions that cannot themselves be statistically verified.

paragraphs: Hyperspectral images contain rich information across spectral bands, supporting applications such as environmental monitoring and precision farming. That richness comes with multiple sources of degradation. Restoring these images is especially difficult because accurate clean measurements taken at the same location are often unavailable, making it hard to assemble the training targets needed by deep restoration models.

The paper proposes a hybrid spectral and spatial sparse coding approach. Its design combines the interpretability of classical methods with parameters that can be learned end to end. Handcrafted image priors encode domain knowledge, while training adjusts the model to the restoration problem. This gives the method a structured starting point without requiring massive amounts of training data.

On several denoising benchmarks, the authors report computational efficiency and substantial improvements over the state of the art. These findings support combining explicit image knowledge with trainable components when clean hyperspectral training data are scarce. The reported evidence concerns denoising, within the broader goal of hyperspectral image restoration.
neurips-2021-a-trainable-spectral-spatia.tldr: A trainable sparse coding model combines image priors with end-to-end learning to restore hyperspectral images efficiently with limited training data.

paragraphs: Point cloud registration aligns shapes represented by collections of points. This can involve matching incomplete views of an object or tracking complex deformations. The paper investigates robust optimal transport as a tool for this problem, showing how modern transport solvers can improve registration methods based on both direct optimization and deep learning.

The work combines a practical account of optimal transport with solutions to difficulties that arise when applying it to shape matching. Transport supports both fast initial alignment and subsequent refinement. The authors evaluate these enhanced models on rigid alignment of partial shapes, scene flow estimation on Kitti, and deformable alignment of lung blood-vessel trees between inhalation and exhalation.

The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy and scalability on Kitti and the lung registration task, with improvements available at an affordable computational cost. They also introduce PVT1010, a public dataset containing 1,010 pairs of densely sampled lung vascular trees. Its complex shapes and deformations provide a challenging resource for studying registration beyond simple rigid motion.
neurips-2021-accurate-point-cloud-regist.tldr: Robust optimal transport improves point cloud alignment across several settings, with leading reported results on Kitti and lung vascular registration.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can perform well during training yet struggle when its environment changes. Data augmentation can help, but different tasks benefit from different transformations of their training inputs. Selecting an effective transformation therefore often depends on expert knowledge. This paper studies how to automate that selection so augmentation can better support generalization.

The authors introduce three approaches for finding useful augmentations and combine them with two new regularization terms. These terms act on the policy and the value function, the two components used by actor-critic algorithms. According to the paper, this regularization is required to make augmentation theoretically sound in that setting, connecting the choice of transformed inputs to the learning objective.

The resulting method achieves a new state of the art on Procgen and outperforms popular reinforcement learning algorithms on DeepMind Control tasks containing distractors. The learned policies and representations also become more robust to environmental changes irrelevant to solving the task, such as background changes. These findings connect automated augmentation selection with improved resistance to distracting visual variation.
neurips-2021-automatic-data-augmentation.tldr: Automatically selected augmentations, combined with policy and value regularization, improve reinforcement learning generalization and robustness to irrelevant environmental changes.

paragraphs: Vision transformers process images through patch-based tokens and self-attention. This paper identifies a problem introduced by the discontinuities in that patch division: jagged artifacts can appear in attention maps. The authors analyze these artifacts as aliasing, where discrete representations create distortions that make some visual information difficult to distinguish.

To address the issue, they propose an Aliasing-Reduction Module, or ARM. The module is designed to be lightweight and easy to insert into existing vision transformers. Its purpose is to bring anti-aliasing properties into these architectures, directly addressing an artifact associated with their image representation. This makes the proposed change applicable across transformer families rather than tying it to one model.

The authors test ARM across multiple tasks and several vision transformer families. They report consistent performance improvements over the evaluated architectures, alongside gains in data efficiency and robustness. The findings suggest that attention-based image models benefit from explicitly addressing aliasing, even though their architecture differs from the convolutional networks where this issue has also been observed.
neurips-2021-blending-anti-aliasing-into.tldr: A lightweight anti-aliasing module reduces patch-related artifacts and improves performance, data efficiency, and robustness across tested vision transformers.

paragraphs: An optimization algorithm's running time depends on both how many iterations it needs and how expensive each iteration is. This paper focuses on the second factor for conditional gradient methods. A major bottleneck is maximum inner product search, which ordinarily requires a scan whose cost grows linearly with the number of parameters.

Approximate search data structures had already been useful as practical shortcuts, but their combination with conditional gradient methods lacked a theoretical framework. The authors provide one using approximate maximum inner product search based on locality-sensitive hashing. The contribution is to formally connect these search tools to optimization algorithms, making their use more than an empirical heuristic.

The resulting algorithms have per-iteration costs that grow sublinearly with the number of parameters for several important methods, including Frank-Wolfe, herding, and policy gradient. This changes the computational scaling of an individual update. The stated advance concerns that update cost, one of the two components governing total optimization time, and offers a complementary direction to reducing iteration counts.
neurips-2021-breaking-the-linear-iterati.tldr: A theoretical framework for approximate inner product search gives several conditional gradient algorithms sublinear per-iteration costs.

paragraphs: Robustness certificates have mostly been developed for classifiers or models producing a single real number. Many useful models instead output objects such as sets, images, or language. This paper extends certification to these structured outputs by expressing output changes through a distance or similarity function appropriate to the application.

The approach treats the output space as a metric space and builds on randomized smoothing. Its center smoothing procedure produces models with a guarantee: for any input perturbation within a specified norm bound, the output changes only by a bounded amount under the chosen output measure. The meaning of robustness therefore depends on both the permitted input change and how output differences are measured.

The authors apply the method to varied output spaces, including sets and images, and report meaningful certificates without substantially reducing the base models' performance. This broadens the kinds of predictions for which provable stability can be studied. The guarantee concerns controlled output change under bounded perturbations, which fits structured predictions whose differences cannot be summarized by a changed class label.
neurips-2021-center-smoothing-certified-.tldr: Center smoothing certifies bounded changes in structured outputs under norm-bounded adversarial changes to the input.

paragraphs: Compressing a neural network requires deciding how much to shrink each layer while meeting an overall size target. This paper presents a framework that makes those decisions jointly across the network. It analyzes individual layers to allocate compression, treating the overall budget and the errors introduced within layers as parts of one optimization problem.

The method divides the channels of convolutional or fully connected layers into groups and applies low-rank decomposition to each group. It derives layer-specific error bounds using the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem. Those bounds then support an objective that minimizes the largest compression error among the layers, with an efficient algorithm proposed to pursue a solution.

This formulation makes the distribution of compression error an explicit design concern, instead of considering only the final model size. Experiments indicate that the method outperforms existing low-rank compression approaches across a range of networks and datasets. The results support studying compression as a global allocation problem, where the choices made for individual layers collectively determine the size and performance trade-off.
neurips-2021-compressing-neural-networks.tldr: A global compression framework allocates layerwise low-rank decompositions to meet a size target while minimizing the largest layer compression error.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks encode how their features should respond to geometric transformations. Ordinary convolutional networks already incorporate translation equivariance, while group-equivariant networks extend this idea. The paper addresses two challenges in those extensions: feature aggregation that is insensitive to spatial context and high computational cost.

The authors introduce a common framework containing both group-equivariant convolutions and equivariant self-attention. They split feature aggregation into a kernel generator and an encoder, and separate computation over spatial dimensions from computation over additional geometric dimensions. This produces dynamic filters. Their model, E⁴-Net, combines equivariance with parameter, computational, and data efficiency; complexity analysis supports the first two efficiency claims, while experiments support the third.

The experiments show improvements over earlier approaches with smaller models. In the specific setting of training on one fifth of CIFAR10, the authors report an accuracy improvement of more than 5% over group-equivariant CNNs while using 56% of their parameters and 68% of their floating-point operations. This example demonstrates the reported benefits under a restricted training-data budget.
neurips-2021-efficient-equivariant-netwo.tldr: E⁴-Net uses dynamic equivariant feature aggregation to improve accuracy while reducing parameters and computation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Training restricted Boltzmann machines requires approximating a likelihood gradient through sampling. This paper focuses on mixing time: how many sampling iterations are needed to obtain genuinely new configurations from the model. The authors show that the relationship between this time and the number of sampling steps used for each gradient approximation strongly affects learning and model behavior.

They distinguish equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium training regimes. Empirically, mixing time increases during learning, so a fixed sampling budget can eventually become too short. With small step counts in contrastive divergence or persistent contrastive divergence, fitted models often have very slow dynamics dominated by nonequilibrium effects. Models trained in equilibrium instead show faster dynamics and smoothly approach configurations resembling the data during sampling.

The practical choice depends on the goal. Short sampling runs can produce convincing samples after brief training, whereas learning the correct equilibrium distribution requires large or increasing step counts. The authors also suggest that these two regimes may occur more generally in energy-based models trained by likelihood maximization.
neurips-2021-equilibrium-and-non-equilib.tldr: The balance between mixing time and sampling budget separates RBM training into regimes suited to different modeling goals.

paragraphs: Self-distillation trains a network using predictions from another network with the same architecture, often alongside the original labels. It has been observed to improve generalization. This paper investigates why the weight assigned to those original targets matters, studying repeated self-distillation in a kernel regression setting.

The analysis considers nonlinear function fitting with a weighted squared-error objective and an ℓ₂ penalty on model parameters. Each distillation step combines model predictions with ground-truth targets. Within this setting, the authors show that the resulting function can be calculated directly from the initial fit. They also show that infinitely many distillation steps correspond to the original optimization problem with stronger regularization.

These results explain how repeated distillation changes regularization and why retaining weighted ground-truth guidance matters. The authors derive a closed-form optimal weighting parameter at each step in their analysis. They additionally show how to estimate that weight efficiently for deep learning, substantially reducing computation compared with grid search. The theoretical characterization is established in the stated kernel regression setting.
neurips-2021-even-your-teacher-needs-gui.tldr: A kernel regression analysis explains self-distillation as amplified regularization and derives how to weight ground-truth targets at each step.

paragraphs: Adversarial training is a promising way to make neural networks more resistant to adversarial attacks. Yet the training procedure leaves an architectural question: how should the network's width and depth be arranged? This paper investigates those choices, focusing on how architecture affects robustness in adversarially trained networks.

The study reports three main observations. Increasing the total parameter count does not necessarily improve robustness. Reducing capacity in the final group of network blocks can actually help. And when the total parameter budget is fixed, the allocation of that capacity admits an optimal architectural configuration for robustness in the studied setting. These findings make the placement of parameters a central consideration.

The authors also provide theoretical analysis explaining why such a configuration can improve robustness. Together, the analysis and observations suggest that robust architecture design should consider where capacity is used, alongside how much capacity is available. The findings concern adversarially trained networks and support deliberate choices about width and depth when designing them.
neurips-2021-exploring-architectural-ing.tldr: In adversarially trained networks, how capacity is distributed across width, depth, and stages can matter more than simply adding parameters.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods can struggle when actions have many dimensions or a task contains many objectives. One reason is the quadratic growth of variance in score-based gradient estimators. This paper develops factored policy gradients to exploit structure in which action components influence which targets, making that structure part of the learning method.

The approach introduces an action-target influence network and uses its encoded independence relationships to construct a factor baseline. The resulting framework generalizes traditional policy gradients and offers a way to incorporate prior knowledge about a domain's generative processes. The authors analyze the estimator and identify conditions under which its variance is reduced.

They also examine how to factor the policy optimally, characterizing this through minimum biclique coverings, a graph-based grouping problem. Incorrectly specifying the influence network affects the balance between bias and variance, making the assumed structure consequential. Experiments show performance advantages on large-scale bandit and traffic intersection problems, with a spatial approximation introduced for the traffic setting.
neurips-2021-factored-policy-gradients-l.tldr: Factored policy gradients use action-target independence structure to reduce gradient variance under identified conditions and improve learning on tested large-scale tasks.

paragraphs: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning learns across tasks, raising two different generalization questions: how well does it perform when a familiar task returns, and how well does it transfer to an unseen task? This paper analyzes both in supervised learning, using a setting with m training tasks and n data points for each task.

For a test task that is one of the training tasks, the authors bound expected excess population loss by O(1/(mn)) when the objectives are strongly convex. This result makes the roles of task count and samples per task explicit. For an unseen task, the generalization error depends on the total variation distance between its underlying distribution and the distributions of the training tasks.

The proofs use algorithmic stability, connecting sensitivity to training data with generalization. The authors introduce a stability definition tailored to meta-learning that captures both m and n. The analysis separates improved estimation on recurring tasks from transfer to new distributions, where the relationship between training and test tasks becomes part of the guarantee.
neurips-2021-generalization-of-model-agn.tldr: A stability analysis bounds MAML generalization on recurring tasks and relates unseen-task error to distributional distance from training tasks.

paragraphs: Imitation learning uses expert demonstrations to guide an agent's behavior. This paper organizes that problem around the expert's occupancy measure, a distribution describing where the expert spends its experience. The proposed framework first estimates the density of that distribution, giving the learning process an explicit model of the expert's pattern of occupancy.

The estimated density then serves as a reward for Maximum Occupancy Entropy Reinforcement Learning. This creates a two-stage route from demonstrations to an imitation policy: learn the expert density, then use it within a model-free reinforcement learning objective. The objective is non-adversarial. The authors also prove a lower-bound relationship between it and reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence between expert and imitator occupancy measures.

The practical algorithm implementing this framework is Neural Density Imitation, or NDI. It achieves state-of-the-art demonstration efficiency on the evaluated benchmark control tasks. The result supports density estimation as a useful foundation for imitation, with the empirical contribution centered on learning effectively from demonstrations and the theoretical contribution connecting the objective to occupancy-distribution comparison.
neurips-2021-imitation-with-neural-densi.tldr: Neural Density Imitation learns an expert occupancy density and uses it as a reward, achieving leading demonstration efficiency on benchmark control tasks.

paragraphs: Adding tree search to a trained reinforcement learning agent can unexpectedly reduce performance, even with exact future states and rewards. The authors trace this to distribution shift: search reaches regions where the pretrained value function is inaccurate. They analyze the phenomenon using Extreme Value theory, explaining why additional search can expose harmful estimation errors.

Their remedy is an off-policy correction that penalizes undersampled trajectories and accounts for the mismatch between the pretrained value function and the search policy. They prove that it removes this mismatch and bound the probability of selecting a suboptimal action. On Atari, the correction substantially improves pretrained Rainbow agents without retraining, often more than doubling their scores.

The paper also introduces Batch-BFS, which uses a GPU to advance all tree nodes at the same depth together. It reduces runtime by two orders of magnitude, making previously infeasible search depths usable for training. DQN agents trained with tree search improve on several Atari games compared with both original DQN and Rainbow.
neurips-2021-improve-agents-without-retr.tldr: An off-policy correction makes tree search improve pretrained agents, while GPU breadth-first search greatly reduces its runtime.

paragraphs: Sprite-based animations are assembled from reusable textured patches representing characters and objects. MarioNette studies the reverse process: recovering recurring graphic elements from the finished animation. Its goal is to turn video content into an explicit representation of reusable pieces and their placement, using self-supervision rather than labeled examples of those components.

The method jointly learns a dictionary of patches and a network that places them on a canvas. Patches can include transparency, allowing the representation to capture elements that do not fill their entire rectangular area. Learning the dictionary and placement process together connects what the recurring elements look like with how they are arranged to form the animation.

The resulting representation is described as sparse, consistent, and disentangled, making its elements accessible for editing or analysis. The contribution is a way to expose reusable structure within sprite-based content. The authors also present the framework as a promising direction for discovering recurring visual patterns in image collections without supervision, extending the motivation beyond its animation setting.
neurips-2021-marionette-self-supervised-.tldr: MarioNette learns reusable patches and their placement from sprite animations, producing an explicit representation for editing and analysis.

paragraphs: Research on neural networks as models of mouse visual cortex has produced mixed conclusions. This paper builds a large benchmark to clarify those findings. It compares dozens of networks against natural-scene responses from more than 6,000 reliable rodent visual cortical neurons in the Allen Brain Observatory's two-photon calcium-imaging dataset.

The benchmark uses both neural regression and representational similarity analysis, examining predictions of individual neuronal activity alongside relationships across population representations. It also broadens the model pool beyond convolutional object recognition systems to include vision transformers, MLP-Mixers, normalization-free networks, Taskonomy encoders, and self-supervised models. This makes architecture, training task, and comparison method part of the investigation.

The authors replicate earlier findings, resolve previous discrepancies, and conclude that modern networks explain mouse visual activity better than earlier results suggested. They offer preliminary answers about individual-versus-population prediction, useful model properties, and correspondence between artificial and anatomical hierarchies. The benchmark provides a reference for further study while keeping those broader biological interpretations exploratory.
neurips-2021-neural-regression-represent.tldr: A broad benchmark finds that modern neural networks explain mouse visual cortical activity better than previous mixed evidence suggested.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning needs useful feature representations, but learning them is difficult when an agent has little experience. Rarely visited or entirely unvisited state-action sequences offer little direct training data. PlayVirtual addresses this problem by generating virtual trajectories that provide additional structure for learning features from limited interaction.

The method operates in a latent space. A forward dynamics model predicts future states from a current state and actions, while a backward model predicts the preceding states. Together they form a cycle. By varying the actions, PlayVirtual creates many virtual trajectories and constrains the forward and backward predictions to be consistent with one another, without requiring ground-truth states for those trajectories.

This consistency requirement supplies a learning signal for the generated sequences, linking imagined transitions to the representation being trained. The authors validate the design on Atari and the DeepMind Control Suite and report state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks. The findings support virtual trajectory augmentation as a way to improve data efficiency in reinforcement learning feature learning.
neurips-2021-playvirtual-augmenting-cycl.tldr: PlayVirtual improves reinforcement learning data efficiency by training representations with virtual trajectories constrained to agree forward and backward.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders describe complex data through lower-dimensional latent variables. When posterior collapse occurs, the posterior over those variables equals the prior, undermining their usefulness as learned representations. This paper examines collapse through latent-variable identifiability: whether the generative model makes the latent variables distinguishable.

The authors prove that posterior collapse occurs if and only if the latent variables are non-identifiable in the generative model. This reframes collapse as a property of the model, extending beyond explanations based on neural networks or approximate optimization. They also demonstrate that classical probabilistic models can exhibit collapse even when inference is exact.

Based on this analysis, the paper introduces latent-identifiable variational autoencoders that enforce identifiability while retaining flexibility. The construction uses bijective Brenier maps parameterized by input-convex neural networks, without special inference objectives or optimization tricks. Across synthetic and real datasets, the proposed models outperform existing methods at mitigating collapse and producing meaningful representations. The contribution links a structural explanation of the failure to an architectural way of addressing it.
neurips-2021-posterior-collapse-and-late.tldr: The paper connects posterior collapse to latent-variable non-identifiability and designs identifiable variational autoencoders that mitigate it.

paragraphs: Transformers can require enormous parameter counts, while dot-product attention has quadratic computational complexity. This paper investigates approximating their two central components, multi-head self-attention and point-wise feed-forward transformations, with fewer parameters and less computation. The approach draws on the interpretation of deep networks as numerical solvers of ordinary differential equations.

The authors use an analogy between transformer stages and the evolution of a system of interacting particles. They develop a temporal evolution scheme that bypasses costly dot-product attention across multiple stacked layers. This dynamical perspective supplies a way to redesign the repeated transformations, with the degree of approximation tied to the extent of parameter reduction.

Experiments cover both encoder-decoder and encoder-only tasks. The effect of approximation differs by task: the proposed scheme achieves performance comparable to the original transformer in the encoder-decoder setting, while consistently outperforming it and several later variants on the tested encoder-only tasks. These results make task dependence central to understanding how much approximation is useful.
neurips-2021-redesigning-the-transformer.tldr: A dynamical-systems-inspired transformer approximation reduces parameters and computation, with task-dependent results across encoder-decoder and encoder-only settings.

paragraphs: Distributed reinforcement learning uses parallel computation, but expressing and combining its algorithms creates programming challenges. This paper revisits those challenges through distributed dataflow: organizing computation around the movement of data between processing stages. The authors argue that this perspective supports implementations that are both performant and easier to compose.

They introduce RLlib Flow, a programming model combining actors with dataflow. Its purpose is to provide a common structure for implementing distributed reinforcement learning algorithms and combining their components. To test whether the model works beyond isolated examples, the authors port the full algorithm suite of RLlib, a widely adopted distributed reinforcement learning library.

The reported results include two- to ninefold code savings in production implementations. RLlib Flow also lets end users compose multi-agent algorithms in ways that were previously unavailable to them. These outcomes concern the software structure used to build reinforcement learning systems: the contribution is an implementation and composition model, with practicality demonstrated across an existing library's algorithms.
neurips-2021-rllib-flow-distributed-rein.tldr: RLlib Flow combines actors and distributed dataflow to make reinforcement learning implementations more compact and composable.

paragraphs: The choice of step size can make an optimization method harder to implement when it requires curvature information or estimates of local smoothness. This paper studies a simple Frank-Wolfe variant for objectives with generalized self-concordance, a property present in many learning problems. Its step size follows the predetermined rule γₜ = 2/(t+2).

For this class of functions, the authors establish an O(1/t) convergence rate in both the primal gap and the Frank-Wolfe gap. These provide two measures of progress toward an optimum. The analysis shows that the fixed schedule can achieve the stated rate without using second-order information or estimating the local smoothness parameters required by previous work.

The paper also proves improved rates in several common settings, including feasible regions that are uniformly convex or polyhedral. These stronger results depend on the geometry of the constraint set. The contribution is therefore both a simple step-size strategy with a guarantee for generalized self-concordant objectives and a characterization of circumstances where convergence can be faster.
neurips-2021-simple-steps-are-all-you-ne.tldr: A simple predetermined Frank-Wolfe step schedule achieves O(1/t) convergence for generalized self-concordant objectives, with faster rates in additional settings.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent can regularize learning through its optimization behavior, even without an explicit penalty. This paper compares that implicit effect with ridge regression's explicit regularization in linear least squares. The analysis covers both underparameterized and overparameterized settings and makes comparisons for individual problem instances within a broad high-dimensional problem class.

For every instance in that class and every ridge parameter, averaged, unregularized SGD generalizes at least as well as ridge when given logarithmically more samples and a suitably tuned constant step size. This is a conditional comparison: the extra samples and step-size tuning are part of the result. It establishes a strong relationship between the two approaches without claiming equal performance at identical sample counts.

Conversely, the authors identify instances where even optimally tuned ridge needs quadratically more samples to match SGD. Together, the results show that SGD can be competitive up to logarithmic factors and substantially better on some problems. They demonstrate that algorithmic regularization has meaningful consequences even in convex linear regression.
neurips-2021-the-benefits-of-implicit-re.tldr: For a broad least-squares problem class, tuned averaged SGD matches ridge with logarithmically more samples and can require quadratically fewer on some instances.

paragraphs: Model-agnostic meta-reinforcement learning requires estimating second derivatives of value functions, collected in a Hessian matrix. These estimates are difficult to implement correctly. Repeatedly differentiating an estimated policy gradient can produce a biased Hessian estimate, so applying automatic differentiation repeatedly does not by itself settle the statistical problem.

The paper develops a common framework for estimating higher-order value-function derivatives using off-policy evaluation. It interprets several previous approaches as special cases, allowing their relationships to be examined within one formulation. In particular, the framework clarifies the trade-off between bias and variance in Hessian estimates, making differences between estimation strategies easier to understand.

The same framework leads to a new family of estimators that can be implemented easily with automatic differentiation libraries. The authors report practical performance gains from these estimates. The contribution combines a theoretical organization of existing methods with an implementation route for new ones, connecting the statistical behavior of higher-order estimates to the tools used to compute them.
neurips-2021-unifying-gradient-estimator.tldr: An off-policy evaluation framework unifies higher-order gradient estimators for meta-reinforcement learning and yields easily implemented new estimators with practical gains.
